claims.text: An actively learned machine-learning interatomic potential trained on a limited amount of ab initio data can emulate the relevant ab initio potential-energy surface.
The machine-learning potential can capture the anharmonicity needed for fusion free-energy calculations.
The machine-learning potential can retain electron–vibration coupling contributions.
Enhanced sampling with the surrogate potential enables rapid exploration of the phase space relevant to fusion.
The proposed method will reliably reproduce solid-state free energies near melting.
The proposed method will reliably reproduce liquid-state free energies near melting.
The method will accurately capture vibrational and configurational entropy contributions.
Vibrational and configurational entropy can both contribute to the thermodynamic stabilization of compositionally complex alloys.
Using an actively learned surrogate reduces the number of costly ab initio evaluations required.
The proposed free-energy method will attain accuracy comparable to full ab initio molecular dynamics.
The proposed method will reduce computational cost by at least one order of magnitude relative to explicit ab initio molecular-dynamics workflows.
The proposed method will scale more smoothly for multicomponent systems than TOR-TILD.
The method is applicable to elemental and binary systems near their melting points.
The expected operating window is approximately 100 K below to 100 K above the melting point.
The approach can extend to multicomponent high-entropy alloys when their configurational disorder is represented adequately in the training data.
Highly chemically ordered or extremely complex multicomponent systems may require additional training data to maintain fidelity.
Latent heat and specific heat capacity around fusion will be predicted with accuracy comparable to explicit ab initio molecular dynamics.
First-principles calculations can predict temperature-dependent specific heat capacity in a multicomponent CoCrFeNiTa alloy consistently with established thermodynamic models.
